synopsis: The corpus recommends judging off-road automatic braking through multiple metrics, including detection and missed hazards, nuisance interventions, timing and stopping outcomes, rather than one aggregate score; comparisons require common ground truth and hazard zones [f188, f7818, f5210]. No fleet-statistical acceptance KPIs were found in off-road standards or regulations, and there is no accepted sensor-simulation realism score or agreed simulation-quality metric framework; recommended metrics therefore should not be mistaken for published thresholds [f2603, f92, f8952, f9357, f7818]. Operator acceptance requires task-specific unnecessary-warning and intervention rates, with nuisance interventions weighted equally to missed interventions; these rates require real operations, preferably shadow mode before braking is enabled, because an excellent overall false-positive rate can conceal an unwanted intervention in nearly every loading or dump cycle [f3342, f5931, f11767, f759, f3655]. Coverage and agreement claims need visible gaps, frozen-set comparisons, pre-agreed tolerances and explicit failures: a vendor reports coverage rising from 12% to 87% in six months, but the booklet warns against hiding uncovered cells inside an overall coverage score [f1558, f9880, f6678, f9934]. For a team starting from zero in October 2026, an initial statistical test plan and coverage metrics are considered realistic by mid-2027; the business case should track cost per credible campaign, wall-clock throughput and analyst hours, not merely raw simulated runs [f846, f10748, f10749].
